verifiedClaims.claim: How contingency fees work in Georgia and South Carolina injury claims: no upfront cost, the lawyer paid from the recovery, and what the agreement must say.

verifiedClaims.claim: The contingency fee system allows injury victims to hire experienced attorneys with no upfront costs — the lawyer's fee is a percentage of the recovery, typically 33-40%.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: LII (Cornell Law School): in personal injury cases 'the successful lawyer is typically entitled to around 33% of the recovery amount.' No authoritative source located for 40% as the top of a 'typical' range; percentages commonly step up if the case is filed or tried, and Georgia/S.C. Rule 1.5(c) contemplates different percentages for settlement, trial or appeal.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Legal Information Institute (Cornell Law School), Wex: contingent fee

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) both require written fee agreements.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Ga. RPC 1.5(c)(1): 'A contingent fee agreement shall be in writing and shall state the method by which the fee is to be determined, including the percentage or percentages that shall accrue to the lawyer in the event of settlement, trial or appeal, litigation and other expenses to be deducted from the recovery, and whether such expenses are to be deducted before or after the contingent fee is calculated.' Georgia's rule does NOT require the client's (or the lawyer's) signature and does NOT require the agreement to say what happens to expenses on a loss. S.C. RPC 1.5(c) (Rule 407, SCACR): 'A contingent fee agreement shall be in a writing signed by the client and shall state the method by which the fee is to be determined, including the percentage or percentages that shall accrue to the lawyer in the event of settlement, trial or appeal; litigation and other expenses to be deducted from the recovery; and whether such expenses are to be deducted before or after the contingent fee is calculated. The agreement must clearly notify the client of any expenses the client will be expected to pay.' O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33 and S.C. Code § 15-3-530 are the personal-injury statutes of limitations, not fee-agreement rules.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Ga. RPC 1.5(c) (State Bar of Georgia handbook); S.C. RPC 1.5(c) (Rule 407, SCACR)
verifiedClaims.note: WRONG CITATION on the summary box: the two statutes cited are limitation periods. Rewrite: 'Georgia and South Carolina both require contingent fee agreements to be in writing (Rule 1.5(c) of each state's Rules of Professional Conduct); South Carolina also requires the client's signature.' SC source: https://www.sccourts.org/resources/judicial-community/court-rules/appellate/rule-407/rule-15/

verifiedClaims.claim: A contingency fee is a payment arrangement where the attorney's fee is a percentage of the compensation recovered in your case. You pay nothing upfront, and if the case is unsuccessful, you owe nothing for legal representation.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: LII Wex: contingent fee; Ga./S.C. RPC 1.5(c)
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate definition. Optional: add 'and no costs' to match the firm policy where Roden is the speaker; as written it is a general definition and does not contradict it.

verifiedClaims.claim: Most personal injury attorneys charge between 33.3% (one-third) and 40% of the recovery. The percentage may increase if the case goes to trial because the attorney's investment of time and resources increases at each stage.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: LII: 'typically entitled to around 33% of the recovery amount.' No authoritative source found that 'most' attorneys charge between 33.3% and 40%. Staged percentages are recognized by Rule 1.5(c) ('percentage or percentages ... in the event of settlement, trial or appeal').

Do not attach a percentage to Roden Law.

verifiedClaims.claim: Attorney fees are the percentage of recovery that compensates the lawyer for legal work. Case expenses are out-of-pocket costs like filing fees, expert witnesses, medical records, and depositions. Most firms advance expenses and deduct them from the settlement.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under the contingency fee model, you owe nothing for the attorney's time if the case does not result in a settlement or verdict. Many firms also absorb advanced case expenses, though this varies — always clarify in your fee agreement.

recommendedEdits: Key Takeaways: replace the wrong citations — fee-agreement writing requirement is Rule 1.5(c) of each state's Rules of Professional Conduct, not O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33 / S.C. Code § 15-3-530 (those are limitation periods).

Georgia does not require the client's signature on a contingent fee agreement (Ga. RPC 1.5(c)(1): 'shall be in writing'); South Carolina does ('in a writing signed by the client'). Neither requires the attorney's signature. Fix Step 2 and the Georgia 'Written agreement required' bullet.

Soften every '33.3%-40% typical' statement (KT, FAQ 2, section intro, table) to 'commonly one-third, often higher if suit is filed or the case is tried' — only ~33% is supported by an authoritative source (Cornell LII). Do not state a Roden Law percentage.

Align Roden-voiced fee statements and FAQ 4 with the firm's confirmed policy: 'Fees and costs apply only upon successful recovery. No fees or costs with no recovery.' Qualify the general 'attorney absorbs' statements (Step 5, $50,000 Risk Transfer) since the post itself says expense handling varies by firm.

Georgia 'Expense disclosure' bullet: drop 'what happens to expenses if the case is unsuccessful' (not in Ga. RPC 1.5(c)); SC 'Written agreement' bullet: replace 'client's right to terminate' with the actual 1.5(c) terms incl. notice of expenses the client will be expected to pay.
Replace unsourced '$300-$500 per hour' with 'hundreds of dollars an hour'; rename 'Cornell Law Institute' to Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute.

Optional: workers' compensation fees are capped by statute — Georgia: Board approval required, no fee over 25% of weekly benefits or settlement (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-108(a); https://sbwc.georgia.gov/frequently-asked-questions/workers-compensation-law-faqs); South Carolina: up to 33.3% of compensation, approved by the Commission (S.C. Code Regs. 67-1205; https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/south-carolina/R-67-1205). The post's 33-40% table does not apply to WC claims, and it links the WC page; a one-line caveat under the table would prevent a misleading read.
